purpose: Evidence-anchored, explicitly interpretive comedy/story retrieval cards, not original-film certification
source_policy: Each short anchor must match the unchanged held caption cue; captions do not verify speaker names or delivery

cards.title: The painter's window distraction
cards.setup: While the court waits for its new judge, a painter is more interested in the activity across the alley than the work he has been hired to do.
cards.payoff: Lana's moral outrage meets a series of literal-minded replies, ending in the painter's bleakly practical remark about his own marriage.
cards.analysis: A three-step escalation from voyeurism to deadpan personal disappointment establishes the show's verbal-comedy rhythm before Harry arrives.

cards.title: Bull's word-of-the-month experiment
cards.setup: Bull explains that he compensates for his education by selecting and using a new dictionary word each month.
cards.payoff: The words become increasingly obscure, while his responses confound any straightforward demonstration of learning.
cards.analysis: The comedy combines Bull's sincere self-improvement with extravagant vocabulary deployed in baffling contexts. Treat the exact pronunciations and delivery as unresolved until audio review.

cards.title: Nobody knows who the new judge is
cards.setup: Lana explains that last-minute mayoral appointments left the court unsure who would be assigned there.
cards.payoff: Harry's eventual arrival confronts the staff with a judge they initially struggle to believe actually holds the office.
cards.analysis: The pilot prepares Harry's unorthodox authority by letting uncertainty about the appointment precede his actions.

cards.title: A judge with an old friend named Hacksaw
cards.setup: Harry's familiarity with a person known as Hacksaw punctures expectations of a conventional courtroom judge.
cards.payoff: The exchange emphasizes Harry's ease with the court's unconventional visitors and his personal history.
cards.analysis: A quick outsider-insider reversal that helps establish Harry's style. The held captions alone do not explain the complete relationship.

cards.title: The Kerr case and a cup of coffee
cards.setup: Harry tries an unconventional reconciliation between the people involved in a violent dispute.
cards.payoff: A colleague incredulously asks why the parties were sent out for coffee rather than processed in a conventionally punitive manner.
cards.analysis: Harry's unconventional faith in reconciliation is contrasted with institutional disbelief. The script alone does not substantiate the physical staging of any offscreen encounter.

cards.title: Dan mourns his shirt
cards.setup: The proposed reconciliation appears to have gone disastrously wrong for Dan.
cards.payoff: When the others express sympathy, Dan focuses on the ruined shirt.
cards.analysis: A character-based deflation of a tense courtroom experiment into Dan's personal vanity.

cards.title: The coin of justice
cards.setup: Harry's suitability for the bench is in question, and he unexpectedly introduces a coin into the decision.
cards.payoff: He proposes resolving whether to remain a judge by a coin flip, which immediately favors him.
cards.analysis: The prop turns a serious question about judicial fitness into a knowingly theatrical test of chance.

cards.title: The rigged coin pays off
cards.setup: The same coin is proposed again as an arbiter of the Kerr case.
cards.payoff: The coin's apparently consistent luck is explained by its having heads on both sides.
cards.analysis: A delayed reveal reinterprets the earlier coin trick and signals Harry's use of purposeful showmanship rather than chance.

cards.title: Twenty-seven years worth saving
cards.setup: The Kerr spouses move from accusation toward acknowledging that they still love one another.
cards.payoff: The staff finally recognizes that Harry has helped preserve a marriage with decades of shared history.
cards.analysis: An emotional payoff gives substance to Harry's earlier eccentric courtroom approach; the show alternates broad comedy with sincere sentiment.

cards.title: Harry's Mel Tormé collecting
cards.setup: Harry reveals a highly particular enthusiasm for singer Mel Tormé.
cards.payoff: He jokes about finding a romantic partner who would be impressed by owning the singer's complete recordings.
cards.analysis: An early seed of Harry's musical taste, useful for future cross-episode continuity if separately corroborated in later scripts.

anchors.contains: every record Mel Torme ever made

cards.title: Campaign drudgery and Dan's sprained tongue
cards.setup: The staff is occupied with a large volume of Sullivan campaign flyers and envelopes.
cards.payoff: When asked to lick an envelope, Dan supplies a ridiculous injury-related excuse.
cards.analysis: An exaggerated physical excuse punctures the collective enthusiasm for monotonous campaign work.

cards.title: The campaign ad's stripped-down production
cards.setup: Christine explains how an extravagant campaign commercial was reduced after eliminating its musical score and underwater dream sequence.
cards.payoff: The resulting ad is dominated by talking, while Dan supplies his predictably sexualized take on what should have appeared.
cards.analysis: A satire of political image-making that also provides a compact Dan-and-Christine character exchange.

cards.title: Dan can only imagine one use for correspondence
cards.setup: Roz describes having a male pen pal.
cards.payoff: Dan speculates about sexually explicit letters and pictures, then questions the value of correspondence without them.
cards.analysis: The running contrast between Roz's unexpected tenderness and Dan's one-track innuendo is a useful character-pair dynamic.

cards.title: Roz's accidental pen-pal romance
cards.setup: Alex's mail continued arriving at Roz's apartment after he moved away.
cards.payoff: A threatening forwarding note somehow begins an affectionate and sustained correspondence.
cards.analysis: Roz's abrasive introduction becomes the origin of an unexpectedly gentle relationship, reinforcing her tough-exterior comic persona.

anchors.contains: had my apartment before I moved in

cards.title: Bull's vice-presidential pen pal
cards.setup: Bull mentions having once maintained a correspondence.
cards.payoff: He implies that the exchange ended because his correspondent became vice president.
cards.analysis: A casual, implausibly high-status connection delivered as personal trivia; any specific real-world vice-president identity would require corroboration.

anchors.contains: I had a pen pal once

cards.title: Judge Grimm's hidden safe
cards.setup: A hidden trigger behind old legal books exposes a safe in the judge's office.
cards.payoff: The discovery is instantly undercut when someone recognizes it as an old safe with an existing reputation.
cards.analysis: A mystery-object setup moves the episode's secondary plot into the world of courthouse history and secrets. Physical trigger operation still requires original-film observation.

cards.title: An old court scandal in the safe
cards.setup: The characters learn of rumors that a previous judge accumulated illicit leverage over famous and powerful people.
cards.payoff: The contents of the safe suddenly suggest a scandalous historical treasure trove.
cards.analysis: The dialogue introduces a tantalizing case of institutional corruption as reported rumor, not confirmed in-world historical fact.

cards.title: Roz's dread of an actual meeting
cards.setup: The prospect of meeting Alex threatens a correspondence made safe by physical distance.
cards.payoff: Roz finally admits that her letters contain embellishments.
cards.analysis: The emotional plot uses the gap between curated written selves and personal vulnerability to complicate Roz's usual confidence.

cards.title: Both pen pals send substitutes
cards.setup: The real Roz and Alex have built inflated versions of themselves in their letters.
cards.payoff: Each discovers the other has sent a stand-in to their first meeting, followed by an absurd identity exchange.
cards.analysis: A symmetrical deception payoff where both characters have committed the same act; the manuscript's individual speaker labels and physical blocking remain provisional.

cards.title: Honesty finally makes a real date possible
cards.setup: After the impostor incident, Roz and Alex exchange apologies and compliments about their invented selves.
cards.payoff: They choose to dine together despite admitting that even mundane letter preferences were false.
cards.analysis: A character-driven resolution in which mutual dishonesty creates an opportunity for sincerity; the final food preference is a miniature callback to the false correspondence.

cards.title: The campaign ad has unexpected consequences
cards.setup: The finished political commercial produces reactions inconsistent with Christine's expectations of its presentation.
cards.payoff: A discussion of the duplicated commercial suggests a technical explanation for the public response.
cards.analysis: A production-related twist is being set up, but the selected held-text anchors alone do not establish the exact technical failure. Do not fill in the missing explanation from a guess.
